The Fast-Cash Advances Draining America’s Small Businesses
 
Plus, Ukraine ends a pause on Russian refinery attacks and Binance probes the biggest-ever crypto heist
 
 
John Jauregui, with his wife Jackie, said their company was caught out by the costs of merchant cash advances. DAVID FOUTS FOR WSJ
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Small U.S. businesses are ailing. Firms offering merchant cash advances promise quick relief: cash in 24 hours or less, easy applications, past credit troubles no problem.

 

The catch is that effective finance costs can reach 2,000%. Because cash advances aren’t legally classified as loans, funders evade traditional lending regulations. They withdraw money directly from company bank accounts, daily or weekly, even if that leaves firms short of funds for payroll, inventory or other operating expenses.

 

Many businesses seeking short-term help instead fall into a debt-driven death spiral. A Wall Street Journal analysis found that more than half of the federal bankruptcies filed by small businesses in the first nine months of 2026 owed money to companies that issue MCAs.

• Officials in the U.S., Singapore and Taiwan have grown concerned that a data-center industry executive with close ties to Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang is a Chinese intelligence source.

 

• Ukraine struck an oil refinery in Russia, ending a two-week pause in attacks that came amid heavy pressure from the Trump administration to halt such operations.

 

• Over 95 years, Weil, Gotshal & Manges pioneered modern bankruptcy law. This week, it was forced to turn that expertise on itself.

 

• State election officials and the Trump administration are eyeing one another with extreme suspicion ahead of Tuesday’s midterms, after months of hostile interactions over the procedures for how Americans vote.

 

• Rail safety has become an election issue in Spain after two deadly accidents on the country’s high-speed network revealed systemic shortcomings in its safety systems.

Go inside the U.S. military’s open-ended mission to keep Gulf oil flowing.

 

Under the cover of darkness, American jet fighters catapult off the USS George Washington and make their way toward the Strait of Hormuz to shoot down Iranian cruise missiles and drones aimed at commercial ships. U.S. troops are operating around the clock to maintain the Iranian blockade and protect ships. But the unrelenting pace of flight operations is putting a strain on aircraft and crew members, according to U.S. officials familiar with the missions. Here is what we observed aboard the USS George Washington.

 
 
 

5. MIDTERMS WATCH

 

Washington coverage chief Damian Paletta: The October Surprise came late, but it came big. The Justice Department issued a new wave of subpoenas on Thursday into an investigation over the Senate race in Alaska. Democrats are hoping to flip that seat blue, but they are fending off allegations that campaign staff for Mary Peltola recruited a spoiler into the race to siphon votes away from GOP incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan. Now, even if Peltola wins, Republicans—and the White House—might try to prevent her from taking the seat in January. And voters could also buck the Democrat amid the mounting scrutiny. This all fits into a chaotic finish to these midterm races, with the Senate still very much up for grabs.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Churches are turning their land into affordable housing.

 
 
 

Across the country, churches with shrinking pews or spare acreage are turning to developers to build affordable housing on their own property, a trend known as “YIGBY,” or Yes in God’s Backyard. The goal: sustain their ministries while easing housing shortages. Although there is no official tally of how much church land nationwide could be developed, studies suggest it is vast.

8. THE NUMBER

 
$500 billion
 

Roughly the market value erased from Alphabet on Thursday in the stock’s worst day on record. The 13% slide, driven by discontent with quarterly results in which the Google Services unit missed analyst expectations, weighed on major U.S. stock indexes and fueled a drop in the Nasdaq composite. The selloff amplified mounting investor anxiety that Google’s biggest revenue engine is slowing as AI reshapes how consumers search—and that the costs of the global AI build-out may be outrunning the returns.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Neighbors are feuding over front yard horror shows as Halloween keeps getting scarier.

 

Tensions are flaring in suburbia as Halloween decorations cross the line from festive to nightmarish. Entire front yards are morphing into wastelands of decapitated bodies, with zombies holding bloody axes and severed pig heads. Some Halloween lovers spend thousands of dollars on props that fill their basements or attics for the rest of the year. Now, weary neighbors are pushing back.
